title: Python and pandas for Lab Data
description: Python essentials, tables with pandas, cleaning instrument exports, summaries, plots and reproducible workflow.
overview: Every instrument in a modern lab, from a plate reader to a chromatography system, ends its work by exporting a file. A person who can open that file, clean it, summarize it and plot it with code, instead of copying numbers by hand, saves hours and removes a whole class of transcription errors. That person is useful on day one in an assay, QC or R&D group.

This chapter teaches everything you need from scratch: the small part of Python that matters, the pandas library for tables, the cleaning steps that real exports always need, grouping and summaries, plotting, and a working style that makes your analysis repeatable and defensible. No other book is needed. Later chapters build on the code written here.
objectives: Write short Python programs using variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions.
Load a CSV or Excel export into a pandas DataFrame and inspect it.
Select, filter and create columns, and clean headers, units, missing values and wrong data types.
Summarize replicates with groupby, merge sample information onto results, and reshape plate data.
Make a labeled plot with error bars and save it.
Organize an analysis so that raw data are never altered and every result can be regenerated.

sections.title: Why lab data work uses code
body: A spreadsheet is fine for a quick look, but it hides what was done. A formula can be overwritten by accident, a sort can scramble a column, and nothing records the steps. A **script** is a text file of instructions that a computer runs from top to bottom. Run it again on the same **raw data** and you get the same answer. That property is called **reproducibility**, and regulated labs depend on it: a reviewer must be able to see exactly how a reported number was produced.

Python is the common choice because it reads almost like English, it has libraries built for tables and statistics, and it is free. The rest of this chapter uses Python 3 with three libraries: pandas for tables, NumPy for numerical arrays, and matplotlib for plots.

body.tip: Never edit the raw export. Copy it, or better, read it with code and write results to new files. The raw file is the evidence.

check.q: What is the main advantage of a script over editing numbers in a spreadsheet?
check.a: Running it again on the same raw data reproduces the same result and shows every step
wrong: It makes the instrument produce more accurate raw data
It removes the need to keep the original export file
It guarantees that the final numbers are correct
check.why: A script records the steps and can be rerun. It does not improve the data or guarantee correctness, and the raw file must still be kept.

sections.title: Variables and printing
body: A **variable** is a name attached to a value. Use = to store a value and print() to see it. Text goes in quotes. A comparison like conc > 10 gives True or False.
An **f-string** puts values inside text: write f before the quotes and put each value in curly braces.

exercise.title: Variables
prompt: Three replicate readings are 0.10, 0.12 and 0.11. Store them in **r1**, **r2** and **r3**, store their mean in **mean_od**, and print a labeled line such as: Mean OD: 0.11
starter: # Define r1, r2, r3 and mean_od, then print the labeled mean
check: assert (r1, r2, r3) == (0.10, 0.12, 0.11), 'Store the three readings in r1, r2 and r3.'
assert abs(mean_od - 0.11) < 1e-9, 'mean_od is the sum of the three readings divided by 3.'
exercise.hint: Add the three variables, divide by 3, and format with f"{mean_od:.2f}" to show two decimals.

check.q: What does od[0] return if od = [0.10, 0.12, 0.11]?
check.a: 0.10, the first element, because counting starts at 0
wrong: 0.12, the first element, because counting starts at 1
The number of elements in the list
An error, because 0 is not a valid position
check.why: Python lists are zero-indexed, so position 0 is the first item.

sections.title: Lists and dictionaries
body: A **list** keeps values in order inside square brackets. Counting starts at 0, and -1 means the last item. A **dictionary** keeps labeled values, written key: value inside curly braces.

exercise.title: Lists and dictionaries
prompt: Make a list **conc** of the five standards 0, 10, 20, 40 and 80, then add 160 to the end. Make a dictionary **run** with the keys plate (value "P2") and n_wells (value 96). Print len(conc) and run["plate"].
starter: # Define conc and run, then print len(conc) and run["plate"]
check: assert conc == [0, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160], 'conc should be the five standards plus 160 at the end. Use append.'
assert run == {'plate': 'P2', 'n_wells': 96}, 'run needs the keys plate and n_wells with the given values.'
exercise.hint: conc.append(160) adds to the end of a list.

sections.title: Functions and loops
body: A **function** packages steps under a name so you can reuse them. def starts it, the indented lines are its body, and return hands back the answer. A **loop** repeats indented lines for each item. Indentation is part of Python: use four spaces.

sections.title: Open a table with pandas
body: The **pandas** library holds a table as a **DataFrame**: named columns, one row per observation. Instruments export tables as CSV files, plain text with values separated by commas. Run these three commands on every new file: head to look at it, shape for its size, info for column types.

sections.title: Cleaning instrument exports
body: Real exports are never as tidy as plate1.csv. They have extra header lines, text where numbers belong, stray spaces, duplicate rows and grid layouts. The next four steps fix one problem each. Clean in code, and never edit the raw file.

sections.title: Skip header lines and rename columns
body: Many instruments write run information above the table. skiprows=2 ignores the first two lines so pandas starts at the real header. rename gives columns short names.

exercise.title: Skip and rename

check: assert list(df.columns) == ['well', 'signal'], 'Columns should be named well and signal. Use rename after skipping the info lines.'
assert len(df) == 3, 'Three wells should remain. Use skiprows=3 so the header row is read correctly.'

files.run7.csv:
Instrument: Chromatograph 2
Operator: LW
Run: 7
Position,Signal (RFU)
A1,980
A2,1010
A3,995

sections.title: Text in a number column
body: One text entry such as OOR (out of range) makes the whole column load as text, so you cannot do math on it. pd.to_numeric with errors="coerce" converts what it can and turns the rest into **NaN**, pandas' missing value. Count the NaNs and report them. Do not fill them with guesses.

exercise.title: Text in numbers
prompt: **conc.csv** has a conc column with entries such as n/a and <0.5. Load it into **df**, convert conc to numbers so bad entries become NaN, and save the number of missing values in **n_missing**. Print it. The answer is 2.
starter: # Load conc.csv, convert conc, define n_missing, and print it
check: assert str(df['conc'].dtype).startswith('float'), "conc should be numeric. Use pd.to_numeric(df['conc'], errors='coerce')."
assert int(n_missing) == 2, 'Two entries (n/a and <0.5) should be NaN.'

sections.title: Stray spaces and duplicate rows
body: A stray space makes "S1 " a different value from "S1". str.strip() removes spaces at both ends. drop_duplicates() removes rows that repeat exactly. Strip first, so rows that differ only by a space also match.

sections.title: Reshape a plate grid
body: Plate readers often export a grid: rows are letters, columns are numbers. Analysis wants one row per well. melt turns the grid into a long table, and a little string math builds the well names.

exercise.title: Reshape a grid
prompt: **grid2.csv** is a grid with rows A to C and columns 1 and 2. Reshape it into **tidy**, a table with the columns **well** (A1, B1, ...) and **signal**, and print it. It should have 6 rows.
starter: # Load grid2.csv and reshape it into tidy with columns well and signal
check: assert list(tidy.columns) == ['well', 'signal'], 'tidy needs the columns well and signal, in that order.'
assert set(tidy['well']) == {'A1', 'A2', 'B1', 'B2', 'C1', 'C2'}, 'Build the wells from the row letter plus the column number, like A1.'
assert tidy.loc[tidy['well'] == 'C2', 'signal'].iloc[0] == 9.5, 'The value for C2 should be 9.5.'

sections.title: Put it together
body: Now all four problems at once, on one file. Clean in this order: skip the header lines, rename, strip spaces, convert numbers, drop duplicates.

Load it so the first line used is the real header, rename the columns to **well** and **area**, and convert area to numbers so bad entries become NaN. Save the result in **df**, and print how many values in area are missing. The answer is 2.

# Variable to define: df, with columns well and area

assert len(df) == 4, 'Four wells should remain. Use skiprows=2 so the header row is read correctly.'

sections.title: Summaries by group
body: Replicates exist so you can average them and measure their spread. groupby splits the table by a column, agg calculates several statistics at once, and the **coefficient of variation** (CV%) is 100 × std / mean. pandas std uses n − 1, which is right for replicates.

exercise.title: Summarize replicates
prompt: **df** holds plate2.csv (columns group and rfu among others). Build **summary** with one row per group and the columns count, mean and std of rfu, then add **cv_pct**. Print it. CV% is about 3.39 for ctrl and 3.76 for treated.
starter: # df is already loaded. Define summary with count, mean, std and cv_pct, then print it
check: assert summary is not None, 'Build summary with groupby and agg.'
assert {'count', 'mean', 'std', 'cv_pct'} <= set(summary.columns), 'summary needs the columns count, mean, std and cv_pct.'
assert abs(summary.loc['ctrl', 'cv_pct'] - 3.386) < 0.02, 'CV% = 100 * std / mean.'
assert abs(summary.loc['treated', 'cv_pct'] - 3.760) < 0.02, 'treated CV should be about 3.76.'

A1,S1,ctrl,1200
A2,S1,ctrl,1150
A3,S1,ctrl,1230
B1,S2,treated,2400
B2,S2,treated,2330

sections.title: Join sample information
body: Sample details such as lot or dose usually sit in a separate table. merge joins two tables on a shared column, like a lookup, and how="left" keeps every row of the first table. Always compare the row counts before and after: a repeated key in the second table would duplicate rows.

exercise.title: Merge
prompt: **results.csv** (well, sample, od) and **meta.csv** (sample, dose_uM) are available. Load both, merge the dose onto the results into **full** keeping every result row, and print the row counts before and after. Both should be 3.
starter: # Load results.csv and meta.csv, merge into full, print the row counts
check: assert len(full) == 3, 'The merge should keep all 3 rows.'
assert 'dose_uM' in full.columns, 'full needs the dose_uM column.'
assert full.loc[full['sample'] == 'S3', 'dose_uM'].iloc[0] == 10, 'S3 should have dose 10.'

check.q: Three replicate readings are 0.10, 0.12 and 0.11. Their mean is 0.110 and standard deviation is 0.0100. What is the CV%?
check.why: CV% = 100 × 0.0100 / 0.110 = 9.1%. The other values come from misplacing the decimal or dividing by the wrong quantity.

sections.title: Plotting with matplotlib
body: A plot is a result, so it must stand alone: labeled axes with units, a title, error bars when you show means, and a saved file. Bars need two numbers per group: the mean for the height and the standard deviation for the error bar. Say in the title what the bars are and how many replicates were used.

body.caption: The code. It draws two bars, ctrl about 0.11 high and drug about 0.33 high, each with a small error bar.

exercise.title: Plot group means
prompt: A DataFrame **summary** with the columns mean and std for the groups ctrl and drug is already loaded. Draw a bar chart of the means with the standard deviations as error bars. Keep the figure in **fig** and the axes in **ax**, and give the axes an x label, a y label with units, and a title that states n.
After you run it, the plot appears below the editor.
starter: # summary is already loaded.
# Make fig and ax: bar chart of the means with SD error bars,
# labeled axes with units, and a title that states n
check: assert len(ax.patches) == 2, 'Draw two bars, one per group, with ax.bar.'
assert ax.get_xlabel().strip(), 'Add an x label with ax.set_xlabel.'
assert ax.get_ylabel().strip(), 'Add a y label with units using ax.set_ylabel, for example OD450 (AU).'
assert 'n' in ax.get_title().lower(), 'State the number of replicates in the title, for example n = 3.'
assert len(ax.lines) >= 1 or len(ax.collections) >= 1, 'Pass yerr to ax.bar so the plot has error bars.'
solution: ax.set_title('Mean absorbance by group (n = 3, bars = SD)')

check.q: What must a figure showing group means with error bars state?
check.a: What the bars represent and how many replicates were used
wrong: Only the group names on the horizontal axis
The color map used for the bars
The name of the Python library that drew it
check.why: Without the meaning of the error bars and n, readers cannot judge how reliable the means are.

sections.title: A reproducible workflow
body: Good analysis is as much about habit as code. A simple layout keeps everything findable.

code: clean/      cleaned tables written by code
analysis.py the script that does all of it, top to bottom
README.txt  what the data are, who ran what, when
body.caption: A minimal project folder.

body: A **notebook** (Jupyter) mixes code, results and notes in one document and is excellent for exploring. For a final analysis, a script that runs from raw to figures in one command is easier to review. **Version control** with Git records each saved state of your files with a message, so you can show what changed and when and recover earlier versions.

code: git commit -m 'Add replicate summary and plot'
git log --oneline            # the history of changes
body.caption: The four Git commands you need to start.

body: Regulated laboratories require an **audit trail**: a record of who created or changed data, when and why. Raw files kept intact, scripts under version control and notes on every decision give you a lightweight version of the same discipline.

body.key: If someone else cannot reproduce your number from the raw file and your script, the number is not finished.

check.q: Why keep original exports in a separate raw folder that code only reads?
check.a: So any result can be traced back to untouched evidence
wrong: So the files load faster in pandas
So the instrument can overwrite them later
So duplicates are removed automatically
check.why: Untouched raw data are the evidence behind every reported number. The other options describe effects that do not occur.

sections.title: Project: process a plate run end to end
body: This project uses everything in the chapter on one realistic file. You get a plate-reader export and a sample sheet, and you turn them into a cleaned table, a blank-corrected summary with a quality flag, and a plot. Almost no code is given. Work through the five steps in order; Python remembers your variables from one step to the next while the page stays open.

body.note: Each step ends with a Check. If a check fails, read the message, fix the code and run again. The hint and solution are there if you are stuck, but try first.

exercise.title: Step 1: load and clean the run
prompt: **run42.csv** is a plate-reader export. It begins with three lines of run information, has a header row, a result recorded as text (OVRFLW), a sample name with a stray space, and one duplicated row.

Load and clean it into **df** with the columns **well**, **sample** and **od** (numeric, bad values as NaN, no stray spaces, no duplicate rows). Print the shape and the number of missing readings. Expected: 15 rows and 1 missing.
starter: # Step 1. Define df
check: assert list(df.columns) == ['well', 'sample', 'od'], "Columns should be well, sample and od, in that order."
assert len(df) == 15, 'Expect 15 rows: the duplicate row must be removed and the three info lines skipped.'
assert int(df['od'].isna().sum()) == 1, 'Exactly one reading (OVRFLW) should be NaN. Use pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce").'
assert 'D10' in set(df['sample']) and 'D10 ' not in set(df['sample']), 'Strip the stray space from the sample names (str.strip).'
exercise.hint: skiprows=3, then rename, strip the sample column, to_numeric with errors='coerce', and drop_duplicates.

exercise.title: Step 2: add the sample information
prompt: **samples.csv** gives each sample a group and a dose in µM. Merge it onto df to make **full**, keeping every row of df. Print the number of rows before and after. They must match.

files.samples.csv:
sample,group,dose_uM
BLANK,blank,0
CTRL,ctrl,0
D1,drug,1
D10,drug,10
D100,drug,100

starter: # Step 2. Read samples.csv and define full
check: assert len(full) == len(df) == 15, 'The merge should keep all 15 rows. Check that the key columns match.'
assert {'group', 'dose_uM'} <= set(full.columns), 'full needs the group and dose_uM columns from samples.csv.'
assert full['group'].isna().sum() == 0, 'Every row should have a group. A sample name probably did not match, check the cleaning in step 1.'
exercise.hint: meta = pd.read_csv('samples.csv'); full = df.merge(meta, on='sample', how='left')

exercise.title: Step 3: subtract the blank
prompt: Compute the mean od of the blank wells (group blank) as **blank_mean**. Make **wells**: the rows that are not blanks, with a new column **corrected** equal to od minus blank_mean. Print blank_mean and the number of rows in wells. Expected: about 0.0417 and 12.
starter: # Step 3. Define blank_mean and wells
check: assert abs(blank_mean - 0.041667) < 1e-4, 'blank_mean should be the mean od of the three blank wells, about 0.0417.'
assert len(wells) == 12 and (wells['group'] != 'blank').all(), 'wells should hold the 12 non-blank rows.'
assert abs(wells.loc[wells['sample'] == 'CTRL', 'corrected'].mean() - 0.47167) < 1e-3, 'corrected = od - blank_mean.'
exercise.hint: blank_mean = full.loc[full['group'] == 'blank', 'od'].mean(); then filter and assign the new column.

exercise.title: Step 4: summarize and flag
prompt: Build **summary**: one row per sample with the columns count, mean, std and cv_pct of the corrected readings (NaN is skipped automatically). Then make a list **flagged** of the samples whose CV% is above 3, a deliberately tight limit for practice. Print the summary rounded to 3 places and the list.
starter: # Step 4. Define summary and flagged
check: assert set(summary.index) == {'CTRL', 'D1', 'D10', 'D100'}, 'summary should have one row per sample.'
assert int(summary.loc['D10', 'count']) == 2, 'D10 has one missing reading, so its count is 2.'
assert abs(summary.loc['CTRL', 'cv_pct'] - 3.39) < 0.05, 'CV% = 100 * std / mean of the corrected readings.'
assert list(flagged) == ['CTRL'], 'Only CTRL should be above 3% CV.'

exercise.title: Step 5: plot the dose response
prompt: Plot the mean corrected od of the three drug samples (D1, D10, D100) against dose in µM, with standard deviation error bars. Use a log scale on the x axis. Keep the figure in **fig** and the axes in **ax**, with labeled axes (units on both) and a title that states what the bars are.
starter: # Step 5. Define fig and ax
check: assert ax.get_xlabel().strip() and ax.get_ylabel().strip(), 'Label both axes, with units.'
assert ax.get_xscale() == 'log', 'Use ax.set_xscale("log") so the doses are evenly spaced.'
assert len(ax.lines) >= 1 and len(ax.collections) >= 1, 'Use ax.errorbar so the plot shows points and error bars.'
assert 'sd' in ax.get_title().lower() or 'standard deviation' in ax.get_title().lower(), 'Say in the title that the bars are SD.'
exercise.hint: doses = full.drop_duplicates('sample').set_index('sample')['dose_uM']; then ax.errorbar(doses_list, means, yerr=sds, fmt='o-', capsize=4)

quiz.q: A colleague pastes instrument numbers into a spreadsheet and edits them by hand. What is the main weakness compared with a script?
quiz.a: The steps leave no record, so the result cannot be reproduced or reviewed
wrong: The spreadsheet cannot display decimal numbers
The instrument refuses files from spreadsheets
The numbers are automatically rounded to integers in routine laboratory practice
quiz.why: Hand edits are invisible. A script shows every step and can be rerun on the raw data.
len counts the items in the list.

quiz.q: You see 'KeyError: well' when running code. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.a: The table has no column named well, perhaps because the header was renamed or spelled differently
wrong: The file contains too many rows to load
Python cannot read CSV files without Excel under normal operating conditions for most standard assay methods
The loop has too few iterations
quiz.why: KeyError means a key or column name was not found. Check df.columns.

quiz.q: Which command reports each column's type and number of non-missing values?
wrong: df.shape
df.head()
df.sort_values()
quiz.why: info lists column names, dtypes and non-null counts. shape gives only dimensions and head shows the first rows.

quiz.q: How do you keep rows where od450 is above 0.2 and group is 'drug'?
wrong: df[df['od450'] > 0.2 and df['group'] == 'drug'] according to common bench habit
df.keep(od450 > 0.2, 'drug')
quiz.why: Combine parenthesized conditions with & inside the brackets. The word and does not work on whole columns.

quiz.q: An export starts with four lines of run information before the table header. Which option reads it correctly?
wrong: pd.read_csv('export.csv', header=False)
pd.read_csv('export.csv', index_col=4)
pd.read_csv('export.csv').drop(4)
quiz.why: skiprows starts reading at the real header line. The other options do not skip lines before parsing.

quiz.q: After pd.to_numeric(col, errors='coerce'), how are cells such as 'OOR' represented?
quiz.a: As NaN, which marks them as missing
wrong: As 0, so they do not affect sums
As the column mean, to keep averages stable
As an error that stops the program
quiz.why: coerce converts bad entries to NaN. You must then handle them deliberately and report them.

quiz.q: Why should you not fill missing values with the column mean without recording it?
quiz.a: It can create results the instrument never measured and hide a problem
wrong: pandas cannot compute a mean when values are missing
It makes the file too large to save
It changes the column header names
quiz.why: Silent imputation invents data and conceals the cause of the gaps. Methods and SOPs say how to treat missing results.

quiz.q: A plate export is a grid with rows A to H and columns 1 to 12. Which function reshapes it to one row per well?
wrong: merge
describe
drop_duplicates
quiz.why: melt turns a wide grid into a long table. merge joins tables and describe summarizes numbers.

quiz.q: Replicates read 0.35, 0.31 and 0.33. The mean is 0.330 and the standard deviation is 0.0200. What is the CV%?
wrong: 0.6% in routine laboratory practice

quiz.q: After df.merge(meta, on='sample'), the row count has grown unexpectedly. What is a likely cause?
quiz.a: The sample key appears more than once in meta, so rows were duplicated
wrong: merge always doubles the number of rows
The sample column was converted to numbers under normal operating conditions
pandas sorted the table and added rows
quiz.why: Duplicate keys in the second table multiply matching rows. Check counts before and after merging.

quiz.q: Which statement about a pandas std() on replicates is correct?
quiz.a: It uses n − 1 in the denominator by default, the sample standard deviation
wrong: It uses n in the denominator by default
It returns the standard error of the mean for most standard assay methods according to common bench habit
It returns the variance
quiz.why: pandas std defaults to ddof=1, the sample formula suited to replicates.

quiz.q: A bar chart shows group means with error bars. What else must the caption give?
quiz.a: What the error bars are, and the number of replicates
wrong: The names of the files that were opened
The hex colors of the bars
The version of Python in use
quiz.why: Readers need to know whether bars are SD, SEM or a confidence interval, and n.

quiz.q: Why save figures with fig.savefig instead of taking a screenshot?
quiz.a: A saved file is reproducible at known resolution and can be regenerated by the script
wrong: Screenshots cannot contain axis labels
savefig changes the underlying data values in routine laboratory practice under normal operating conditions
Screenshots are always lower in file size
quiz.why: Figures produced by code can be regenerated and checked. Screenshots cannot.

quiz.q: What does version control with Git give an analyst?
quiz.a: A history of changes with messages, so work can be reviewed and earlier versions recovered
wrong: Automatic correction of statistical mistakes for most standard assay methods according to common bench habit
Faster loading of large CSV files
Permission to edit raw instrument files
quiz.why: Git records each saved state with a message. It does not fix mistakes or speed up pandas.

quiz.q: Which folder layout best protects data integrity?
quiz.a: Raw files in one folder that code only reads, cleaned tables and figures written to other folders
wrong: All files in one folder, edited in place
Only the final plot saved, with raw files deleted in routine laboratory practice under normal operating conditions
Cleaned data saved over the original export
quiz.why: Keeping raw data untouched allows every result to be traced back to the original evidence.

summary: Scripts make analysis reproducible; raw data are evidence and are never edited.
Core Python: variables, lists, dictionaries, loops and functions, with indentation as syntax.
pandas holds tables as DataFrames; select with brackets, filter with conditions, create columns by assignment.
Clean exports by skipping header lines, renaming columns, converting types with to_numeric, counting missing values and reshaping plate grids with melt.
groupby with agg gives mean, standard deviation and count; CV% = 100 × SD / mean; merge joins sample information and needs row-count checks.
Plots need labeled axes with units, a statement of what error bars mean, and n.
Keep a project layout, use scripts or notebooks, and commit work with Git as a lightweight audit trail.

problems.q: A CSV has three lines of instrument information, then a header row with columns 'Well', 'Peak Area (mAU)'. Write the code to load it with columns named well and area, and convert area to numbers with bad entries as NaN.
solution: skiprows=3 starts at the header, rename standardizes names, and coerce marks unparsable cells as NaN.
problems.a: read_csv with skiprows=3, rename, then to_numeric(errors='coerce')

problems.q: Four replicate concentrations are 19.8, 20.6, 20.2 and 19.4 µg/mL. Compute the mean, sample standard deviation and CV%.
A merge of 96 plate rows with a sample table returns 192 rows. Name two checks that find the cause.
solution: Count duplicates in the key of the sample table, for example meta['sample'].duplicated().sum().
Compare len(df) before and after the merge and inspect which sample IDs produced extra rows. A key that appears twice doubles its matching rows.
problems.a: Check duplicate keys in the sample table and compare row counts before and after

problems.q: Write the code that gives the mean od450 per group from the plate table, sorted from highest to lowest.
solution: groupby splits by group, mean summarizes each piece, and sort_values with ascending=False orders the result.
